title: Sound Waves Help Chemo Reach Brain Tumours, Extending Survival by 40 Percent
excerpt: A landmark trial shows focused ultrasound can safely open the blood-brain barrier, delivering more chemotherapy to glioblastoma and boosting survival from 19 to 31 months.
body:
• Glioblastoma patients treated with MRI-guided focused ultrasound plus chemotherapy survived a median of 31.3 months, versus 19.3 months with chemo alone — a nearly 40% improvement.
  • The technique uses microbubbles and sound waves to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier, allowing drugs to reach tumour cells that surgery cannot remove.
  • Follow-on trials are now underway in North America and Asia, with researchers exploring the approach for other brain diseases including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

A clinical trial has demonstrated for the first time that using focused ultrasound to open the blood-brain barrier during chemotherapy can meaningfully extend the lives of patients with glioblastoma, the deadliest form of brain cancer. The results, published in The Lancet Oncology, show that the technique nearly doubled progression-free survival and extended overall survival by approximately 12 months compared to standard treatment alone.

How It Works

Glioblastoma kills most patients within 14 to 16 months of diagnosis, with a five-year survival rate of just 5.5 percent. Even after surgery, residual cancer cells embedded deep in brain tissue inevitably regrow. The blood-brain barrier — a tightly sealed network of cells lining the brain's blood vessels — keeps out toxins but also blocks most chemotherapy drugs. Studies estimate that less than 20 percent of temozolomide, the standard chemo drug for glioblastoma, actually reaches the brain.

The new approach, called microbubble-enhanced transcranial focused ultrasound (MB-FUS), works by injecting tiny gas-filled bubbles into the patient's bloodstream. An MRI-guided ultrasound device then targets precise brain regions with low-intensity sound waves. The bubbles oscillate under the sound energy, temporarily pushing apart the cells that form the blood-brain barrier. With the barrier open, chemotherapy floods into the tumour site at far higher concentrations.

"To think about being able to offer repeated, large-volume blood-brain barrier-opening treatment — and to do this safely in the setting of delivered therapies like chemotherapy — is a remarkably impressive technological advancement in human health and medicine."

— Graeme F. Woodworth, MD, Chair of Neurosurgery, University of Maryland School of Medicine

The Trial Results

The phase 1/2 BT008NA trial, led by Woodworth at the University of Maryland and conducted across five centres in the US and Canada — including affiliates of Harvard University, the University of Virginia, the University of Toronto, and West Virginia University — enrolled 34 adults with newly diagnosed glioblastoma between October 2018 and March 2022.

Each patient had already undergone surgery and six weeks of chemoradiotherapy. They then received up to six monthly sessions of MRI-guided focused ultrasound alongside standard temozolomide. Their outcomes were compared against 195 matched control patients who received temozolomide without ultrasound.

Median progression-free survival reached 13.5 months in the ultrasound group, compared to 8.1 months in the control arm. Overall survival climbed to 31.3 months versus 19.3 months — a gap of 12 months, according to The Lancet Oncology. No treatment-related deaths occurred, and only one adverse event linked to focused ultrasound exceeded grade 2 severity, Healio reported.

Beyond Treatment: A Liquid Biopsy Bonus

An unexpected benefit emerged from the trial. By opening the blood-brain barrier, the technique allowed tumour-derived DNA fragments and other biomarkers to pass from the brain into the bloodstream. Researchers found these circulating biomarkers closely tracked patient outcomes, offering a potential "liquid biopsy" — a simple blood test that could monitor whether the cancer is stable, progressing, or responding to treatment, without invasive procedures.

"This new approach may allow us to create a monthly adaptive diagnostic and treatment paradigm where the residual invasive disease is targeted for treatment and then the treatment can be evolved month to month based on the continually updated circulating biomarker data," Woodworth told Healio.

Global Momentum

The breakthrough is accelerating research worldwide. In Taiwan, a pilot trial at Linkou Chang Gung Memorial Hospital used a portable focused ultrasound device called NaviFUS alongside Avastin (bevacizumab) for recurrent glioblastoma, reporting median progression-free survival of 11 months. That study, published in Neurosurgery in early 2026, has now progressed to a phase III randomised trial enrolling patients across two Taiwanese sites.

In North America, the larger LIBERATE trial is evaluating focused ultrasound for glioblastoma diagnostics, while the University of Maryland has opened a new trial combining the technique with carboplatin, a chemotherapy agent that may be more effective against brain tumour cells once the barrier is overcome. A next-generation dome-helmet device developed at Toronto's Sunnybrook Research Institute is also entering clinical testing.

Researchers believe the same barrier-opening technique could eventually deliver drugs for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and other neurological conditions that have resisted treatment because of the blood-brain barrier.

What's Next

The standard treatment protocol for glioblastoma has remained essentially unchanged since 2005. These new findings provide the strongest evidence yet that focused ultrasound could reshape that standard of care. The next step is randomised controlled trials large enough to confirm the survival benefit and win regulatory approval. Woodworth's team is also working to understand whether the benefit comes purely from increased drug delivery or whether the ultrasound itself activates the immune system against the tumour.

For the roughly 15,000 Americans and over 28,000 Indians diagnosed with glioblastoma each year, the results offer a rare note of genuine progress against a cancer that has long defied medicine's best efforts.
nri_angle: Glioblastoma affects over 28,000 Indians annually, and global trials including centres in Asia could accelerate access to the treatment for patients in India and the diaspora.
